text.p: Amid the deafening clanking of cow bells, the crowd's cheers rise in volume as the ski jumper takes flight before landing at the bottom of the slope.
Norwegians are doing what they like best -- standing on a frozen mountainside watching their sporting heroes.

Forming a sea of red, blue and white -- the colours of the Norwegian flag -- almost 35,000 spectators have flocked to the 1997 Nordic skiing world championships in Norway's second-oldest city of Trondheim.
Undeterred by snow and a heavy downpour of rain, the lively throng roars support for the athletes and between competitions dances and drinks from steaming flasks.

"Everyone is very happy, there's a very good spirit here," said Morten Thrones, 25, from Trondheim. "In the town it's almost like being in the south like in Italy or Spain. Everyone is out and smiling and there are street markets."

Nordic skiing is made up of cross-country events, ski jumping and a combination of the two. Unlike its more glamorous brother, Alpine skiing, it has little following outside the Nordic region -- Denmark, Finland, Iceland, Norway and Sweden -- the countries of the former Soviet Union and Germany, Italy and Japan.

The triumphs in world competition of Norwegian Alpine skiers Lasse Kjus, Kjetil Andre Aamodt and Atle Skaardal have raised the profile of the speedier sport in Norway but it is still Nordic skiing which holds top status among the public.

"Nordic skiing here is like a religion. Everybody follows it and everybody loves it," said Terje Sivertsen, a 54-year-old bank worker from Oslo. "We're a small country and we're very patriotic. We love sport and this is our number one sport."

Sivertsen, sporting a Norwegian flag painted across his nose, requested special leave from his job to attend the championships. He walks six kilometres each morning to catch the shuttle bus to Granaasen, just outside Trondheim, where the competitions are being staged.

Organisers of the 1997 championships say they expect crowds of up to 90,000 next weekend for the final and biggest attractions, the men's 50 kilometres cross-country race and the high hill ski jumping.

It is not difficult to understand the popularity of Nordic skiing. The Scandinavian country of nearly 4.5 million has long, hard winters when large parts of the land are covered in snow and ice and daylight disappears for several months of the year.

While their continental European counterparts hide away when temperatures drop near to freezing, Norwegians flock to the forests and mountains to enjoy around 30,000 kilometres -- three times the distance between Norway and Australia -- of marked ski trails through unspoilt scenery.

Skiing is deeply embedded in Norwegian culture. The word ski comes from the Old Norse word "skid", meaning a split length of wood. Up to 100 years ago, much of community life in winter was dependent on skis for hunting and for getting around in the sparsely populated country, where distances are great and terrain difficult.

But it was Sondre Norheim from the county of Telemark in the southern part of the country who pioneered skiing as a sport in the 1880s. Often referred to as the father of modern skiing, Norheim was the originator of Telemark skis, which are narrower in the middle than at the front and back and have stiff heel bindings.
Norway's modern-day heroes include Bjoern Daehlie, one of the greatest cross-country skiers of all time, who has notched up six world titles, five Olympic golds and a record 35 World Cup wins.

Daehlie had to be satisfied with a silver medal in the opening world championship event, the 30 kilometres freestyle cross-country race on Friday, while compatriot Bjarte Engen Vik was also beaten into second place in Sunday's Nordic combined.
But the crowd's enthusiasm is undiminished. National pride following the successful 1994 Winter Olympic Games in Lillehammer continues to run high.

"The Norwegians, they know how to arrange these kinds of events. They're very friendly and it doesn't matter where the competitors come from, they like them all," said Esa Aaltonaa, 32, from the Finnish capital Helsinki.
